title: TB8-19318
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant is a citizen of India. He worked on board ships as XXXX XXXX from 2008 until 2014 with employers based in Dubai and the U.S. He alleges that he cannot return to India as he made an enemy of a Bhartiya Janata Party (BJP) leader, named XXXX XXXX. The Appellant alleges that in XXXX 2014, he asked Mr. XXXX to leave a family wedding because he was harassing female members of his family and that Mr. XXXX took this as a personal insult. The Appellant left India in XXXX 2014 and travelled to the United States using his seaman documentation. He stayed in the United States illegally for more than two years. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 he entered Canada in an irregular manner. He was arrested, detained and claimed asylum. The Appellant alleges he fears the police, XXXX XXXX, his friends, the BJP in India and that he would not be safe in any part of India.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) determined that the Appellant's allegations lacked credibility and rejected his claim. In the alternative, the RPD reasoned, a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) exists in India. I have determined that the RPD was correct in rejecting his claim due to the Appellant's lack of credibility, which is the determinative issue of the claim. In my opinion, there is no need to assess the possibility of an IFA given that the allegations are not credible. The appeal is dismissed.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.1 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases, may attract deference. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.

I have attentively listened to the recording of the RPD hearing, and have carefully reviewed all of the supporting documentation. I agree with the RPD's decision and find that the determinative issue is the lack of credibility of the allegations.

The RPD determined that the Appellant lacked credibility for several reasons, namely: (a) The Appellant came to Canada after living in the U.S. illegally for 30 months, a country in which he did not file a refugee claim. (b) The Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, signed on May 25, 2017, was significantly different than the reasons he provided for leaving India at his interview with a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officer on XXXX XXXX, 2017 (the day after he entered Canada). At that time, he indicated he left India because of a fight at a wedding, the cause of which was a land dispute, that he was injured in the fight (not his brother, as alleged in his BOC), that he did not go to police to report the problem (which again differs from his BOC) and he makes no mention of his persecutor being affiliated with the BJP. The RPD did not err, the Appellant's allegations are not credible

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in not accepting his explanation for the discrepancies between his BOC and the CBSA interview notes. The Appellant explained at his hearing that he was nervous and scared at the time of his interview with the CBSA because he was detained. The Appellant also submits that "he did experience difficulty to understand the interpreter provided to him." And that "his interview with his CBSA officer was not recorded".2 The Appellant also notes that according to the case law, "evidence which is given by a witness under oath is presumed to be the truth unless it is either (a) contradicted, (b) internally inconsistent, or (c) implausible."3

Firstly, the RPD determined that the Appellant was not credible because his statements were contradicted by earlier statements he made, thus the presumption of truthfulness was firmly rebutted. I find this reasoning to be correct.

Secondly, the RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanations for the discrepancies, as though he acknowledged that the Appellant may have been uncomfortable and likely felt intimidated at the time he was detained, the Appellant did answer numerous questions and provided oral evidence which was substantially different than the information in his BOC. I agree, nervousness and discomfort does not explain why the Appellant would provide different information about the reason he fears returning to India. In the one version, the crux of the problem was a land dispute, in the second version it was because he was defending female members of his family. In one version, he was injured, in another version his brother was injured and the Appellant was not even present when his brother was injured. In one version he went to police to report the problem, in the second version he had no time to report the incident to police as he had to catch a flight. The differences in information are neither peripheral nor microscopic but go to the heart of his claim.

With regards to the fact that the interview with the CBSA officer was not recorded, it is presumed that the officer recorded the questions and answers to the best of her ability and would have no reason to record any information inaccurately.

In terms of the adequacy of interpretation provided by the CBSA, the RPD noted that the Appellant is recorded as indicating that he understood the interpreter.4 I also note that during the hearing, the Appellant, when answering the RPD member's questions made no comment about not understanding the interpreter at his CBSA interview. It was only when questioned by his own Counsel that the Appellant agreed that perhaps he did not fully understand the interpreter at all times. He also indicated, however, that he was able to continue with the interview and that a lack of comprehension was not the reason for the discrepancies in his testimony: Counsel: Just with respect to the Port of Entry notes, MrXXXX XXXX, (...) I ask you about discrepancies between Port of Entry notes and narratives. You are interviewed by Hearing Advisors, when you entered Canada. And it happened on XXXX XXXX 2017. Do you remember? Claimant: Yes Counsel: You were interviewed with the assistance of a Punjabi interpreter, Vinay Kapoor. Claimant: Yes Counsel: Did you ever have any difficulty to understand the interpreter, Mr. Vinay Kapoor? Claimant: Little bit, I did. Counsel: If that's the case, did you bring it to the notice of the officer? Claimant: No. Counsel: Why not? Claimant: I did not know much about it to tell the officer that I was having some problem. Counsel: Why it was so? Claimant: I would not say that I was not completely understanding, but here and there, there were some areas where I did not, but as the questions were being asked I was giving my answers. Counsel: The explanation you provided today with respect to the discrepancies in the Port of Entry notes and narratives, you said, you testify, that it was because you were nervous, you were scared, you forgot some things. That's the sole reason? Claimant: Yes.5
Thus, I do not find that inadequate interpretation at the Appellant's CBSA interview caused the discrepancies with the Appellant's narrative.

Furthermore, I also agree with the RPD that the addition of the BJP element in the BOC as compared with the CBSA interview notes is telling. It adds an element which would aggravate the risk the Appellant would face in India. However, I find that this addition is not credible, not only for the reason that it was missing from the story he told the CBSA officer, but I note that during the hearing the Appellant was not even able to identify how Mr. XXXX was affiliated with the party: Tribunal: Why did XXXX take it so bad? Why would he want to kill you? Claimant: Because he was a leader of the BJP party as well. Because whatever argument or physical fight we had at that gathering, he took it as a personal insult to him. (...) Tribunal: When you say he is a leader, what does that mean? Claimant: There is one party, it is called BJP in Punjab. And he, XXXX XXXX, he was a leader in that area. Tribunal: But, by leader, what does he do? How is he known as a leader? Claimant: By that I mean, that any big leader like MP or MLS, from BJP, whoever could come, they would directly meet up with him or interact with him. Like he had good control because of all the people that he knew and would all come to meet him, so he had a good position. Tribunal: But he is not as high as an MP? Claimant: No, not an MP. Tribunal: What is the source of his influence? What does he do? Claimant: Because he had contacts with MPs and MLS and he could take full support from them and have good contacts with police as well. Tribunal: I see, what I meant was, what is it about him that lets him have these contacts? Is he a rich guy? Claimant: Yes he was rich as well as he knew all the big position people6.

As can be seen from the above excerpt, the Appellant failed to answer the RPD's question as to exactly what role in the party Mr. XXXX played, indicating only he was someone with influence but who was not an MP. The Appellant was not able to explain how this person was considered a "leader" of the BJP. I find that his testimony was evasive on this point and that, like the RPD, this element was added to embellish his claim.

Ultimately, I find that the credibility of the Appellant's allegations is completely undermined by the earlier version of his story he provided to the CBSA officer as well as his testimony before the RPD. The RPD did not err, the Appellant is not credible. The RPD's analysis of a viable IFA was unnecessary.

The Appellant submits that the RPD's IFA analysis was faulty as the BJP is the ruling party in India and therefore it has a national reach. In my opinion, the IFA analysis was unnecessary. There was no need for the RPD to proceed to an "in the alternative" assessment of the evidence as the Appellant was not credible and, in my opinion, the lack of credibility is determinative The RPD did not fail to assess the claim under section 97(1) of IRPA.

The Appellant asserts: "The board member completely failed to assess the claim made by the appellant under section 97 (1) of lRPA as a person in need of protection. The appellant's identity is not disputed, and he has a fear of persecution because he opposes the BJP. The board member made a reviewable error by doing so."7

The Appellant has not explained what aspect of analysis related to section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) he believes was missing in this case. Based on my independent review, I do not find that a section 97 analysis is lacking. The case law provides that a separate s. 97 analysis is not required in all cases and is not required when the claimant's allegations are the same for both s. 96 and s. 97, and they where they were found not to be credible, as in the present case.8 I also note that this the first time the Appellant characterizes himself as someone who "opposes the BJP". There is no evidence before me that this is the case and the Appellant has not applied to have new evidence admitted. The RPD does reference section 97 in his decision9, which means that he did indeed take it into account. The RPD member was therefore satisfied that the Appellant, based on the evidence, would not be personally subjected to a risk of torture, a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he return to India. I am also satisfied on this point based on the lack of credibility of the Appellant.

In terms of section 96 of IRPA, like the RPD, because of the serious problems with credibility, I am not satisfied the Appellant has demonstrated that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted on a Convention ground if he returned to India at this time.

I dismiss the appeal. The Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
